entities.name: Abraham of Cyrrhus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Saint Abraham of Cyrrhus (also known as Abraames, Abraham of Charres, and Abraham the Apostle of Lebanon) was a renowned Syrian hermit, ascetic, and bishop of Harran who lived during the Classical era, particularly in the 4th and early 5th centuries CE. Born around 350 CE in Cyrrhus, a city in northern Syria, Abraham became a prominent figure in early Christian monasticism and spiritual leadership. He dedicated much of his life to hermitic practices and religious contemplation, embodying the ascetic ideals that flourished during the Classical period's philosophical and spiritual inquiry. His spiritual authority and religious teaching made him influential in shaping religious practice and community formation throughout the Eastern Mediterranean and Levantine regions. As bishop of Harran, Abraham played a significant role in the institutional development of the Church and contributed to the codification of Christian doctrine and religious practice. His life and teachings exemplified the fusion of philosophical inquiry and spiritual devotion characteristic of the Classical era. Abraham's works and influence extended beyond his lifetime, shaping the religious frameworks and institutional structures that influenced subsequent Christian civilization. He is venerated as a saint in Christian traditions and remains a significant figure in the history of monastic spirituality and ecclesiastical leadership. Abraham died in 423 CE, leaving behind a legacy of religious devotion, spiritual teaching, and institutional contribution that endured for centuries. His associations with religious communities, comparative religious thought, and cultural diffusion across the Mediterranean world underscore his importance in understanding the development of early Christian doctrine and practice.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Abraham of Cyrrhus was a prominent figure in early Christian monasticism and spiritual leadership, influencing religious practice and community formation throughout the Eastern Mediterranean and Levantine regions. His ascetic ideals contributed to the development of hermitic practices during the Classical period.
